name: Salon Owner
description: A 90-minute, 4-round basic Express simulation on a young licensed stylist's first year owning a four-chair salon suite: choosing booth rent or commission for the other chairs and keeping the line between a renter and an employee (26 CFR §31.3121(d)-1(c)), pricing the service menu from the cost of each service, protecting the appointment book from no-shows with a card on file, a stated cancellation policy and reminders, keeping licensed services in licensed hands with a shampoo-only assistant (O.C.G.A. §43-10-8(a), §43-10-17), disinfecting every tool after every client under the state sanitation rule (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 130-5-.05), applying the no-show policy fairly, setting money aside for taxes and choosing how to grow in year two, for high-school and postsecondary Career and Technical Education in cosmetology and courses preparing the state cosmetology licensing exam. Jalisa Merriweather, 20, the fictional licensed owner of the fictional Velvet Fern Salon Suites in Atlanta, Georgia, runs the salon through 2027 with her former instructor Delphine Strother on the phone. Round by round you decide the business model for the other three chairs and the price menu, how to book against no-shows and who works the Saturday rush, how to disinfect and how to handle a week of no-shows, and how to manage the money and the second year; at each decision point the salon's typical week is projected again with the decisions taken so far. Each round is scored on completed appointments, the owner's hours over a 50-hour week, the no-show rate, the weekly profit and client loyalty, with open violations shown alongside; running booth renters like employees or letting an unlicensed person do color caps the score. English with Spanish.
view:
Salon Owner

One 20-year-old licensed stylist, a four-chair salon suite in Atlanta and its first year: choose booth rent or commission for the other three chairs, price the menu, protect the book from no-shows, keep unlicensed hands off licensed services, pass the inspection, set money aside for taxes and decide how to grow.

Jalisa Merriweather · owner · Velvet Fern Salon Suites · Atlanta, Georgia · 2027 You are Jalisa Merriweather, 20, a licensed cosmetologist. You finished cosmetology school, passed the state board exam, worked two years behind someone else's chair, and in December 2026 signed the lease on Velvet Fern Salon Suites, a four-chair salon suite in Atlanta's West End. The salon is registered with the state board and opens on Saturday 16 January 2027. You work the first chair; three licensed stylists want the other three. Your former instructor, Ms. Delphine Strother, answers your calls. Each round is scored on the salon's typical week as projected at that moment: completed appointments, your hours over a 50-hour week, the no-show rate, the weekly profit and your clients' loyalty.

Round 1 — January: the business model and the menu

Monday 4 January 2027, before the opening. Tavia Okonkwo-Bell wants a lease at a weekly rent and her own clients; Bastien Ruddock would rather be paid a commission with a steady schedule; Mireille Duchamp-Hayes asks whether she can be "a renter, but you handle the products and the booking". A friend from school says to "just call them renters, take a cut and skip the payroll — everybody does". The menu is blank. The four chairs can take about 120 appointments a week.

Deliverable: the one-page chair agreement for one stylist, and the costing of one service on the menu. This round is scored on the salon's typical week as projected now; your later decisions are assumed at current practice.

Round 2 — April: the book and the Saturday rush

Monday 5 April, three months in. Saturdays are booked solid and the waiting list is long; on weekdays about one appointment in five ends as a no-show. Your cousin Shontae, 22, "great with color" but unlicensed, offers to do color on Saturdays for cash. Philippa Trevathan, a licensed stylist, would rent the empty chair by the day on Saturdays; Marcus Ebo, 18, wants a few Saturday hours shampooing.

Deliverable: the cancellation policy as clients will read it, and the Saturday staffing plan with each person's license status. Scored on the salon's typical week as projected now.

Round 3 — July: the inspection and the no-show week

Tuesday 6 July, the week after the holiday weekend: five no-shows in two days. A client has posted a photo of a comb taken from one station and used on the next client, and an inspector of the state board walks in unannounced. Georgia's rule: every multi-use tool cleaned and disinfected after each use, by complete immersion for at least 10 minutes in an EPA-registered, hospital-grade disinfectant, the solution changed daily, clean tools in a covered, labeled container (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 130-5-.05).

Deliverable: the daily disinfection checklist, and the message to a client who missed her appointment. Scored on the salon's typical week as projected now.

Round 4 — October: the money and year two

Monday 4 October. The September estimated-tax payment has come and gone. The landlord offers an eight-chair salon two doors down; a product rep offers a $3,000 retail order; Mrs. Ottilie Lumpkin, a regular since January, says the prices are fair and the chair is never late.

Deliverable: the weekly money routine on one page, and the year-two decision with its numbers. This round is scored on the salon's week as the first year closes.

summary.en: You are Jalisa Merriweather, 20, a licensed stylist in her first year owning Velvet Fern Salon Suites, a four-chair salon in Atlanta's West End. You choose booth rent or commission for the other three chairs, price the services and guard the book against no-shows.
summary.es: Eres Jalisa Merriweather, estilista con licencia de 20 años, en tu primer año como dueña de Velvet Fern Salon Suites, un salón de cuatro sillones en el West End de Atlanta. Eliges alquiler o comisión para los otros tres sillones, fijas los precios y proteges la agenda de las ausencias.

text.en: Compare booth-rent and commission models on profit, hours and risk, and keep the legal line between a chair renter and an employee
text.es: Comparar los modelos de alquiler de sillón y de comisión en beneficio, horas y riesgo, y respetar la frontera legal entre un arrendatario de sillón y un empleado

text.en: Design an appointment-book policy against no-shows with a card on file, a policy stated at booking and reminders, applied to every client the same way
text.es: Diseñar una política de agenda contra las ausencias con tarjeta registrada, una política comunicada al reservar y recordatorios, aplicada a todos los clientes por igual

text.en: Apply sanitation and licensing rules every day, keeping licensed services in licensed hands and disinfecting every tool after every client
text.es: Aplicar cada día las normas de higiene y de licencias, reservando los servicios con licencia a personal con licencia y desinfectando cada herramienta después de cada cliente

text.en: Calculate service prices from product, time and rent, and grow on purpose through a price rise for new clients and rebooking before taking a bigger lease
text.es: Calcular el precio de cada servicio a partir del producto, el tiempo y el alquiler, y crecer con intención mediante una subida para clientes nuevos y la repetición de citas antes de firmar un local mayor

text.en: Plan the salon's money with a separate business account, a set share of every week put aside for taxes and books kept weekly
text.es: Planificar las finanzas del salón con una cuenta separada, una parte fija de cada semana reservada para impuestos y la contabilidad al día cada semana
